title: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
desc: Finds convergence around verification, task boundaries and security, with approval and disclosure producing the clearest jurisdictional differences.

kps.k: Courts are converging on an assistive, human-accountable model of AI use.
kps.d: The central proposition permits AI to support research, drafting, summarisation, document review and administration, but keeps professional responsibility and adjudicative authority with lawyers, judges and court users. Judicial guidance commonly bars delegation of decisions, requires judges to engage directly with evidence and treats AI output as provisional rather than authoritative. Existing legal, ethical and procedural duties continue to apply; AI does not create a defence for defective work.

qs.q: AI                                          is envisaged not as a replacement for judicial reasoning, but as an                                          assistive tool to expand access to information, enhance efficiency,                                          and support equitable justice—always under meaningful human su-                                          pervision and ethical review.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Verification is the principal operational safeguard, but it must be independent and proportionate to the task.
kps.d: Policies require humans to check accuracy, completeness, currency, jurisdictional relevance, citations, quotations and bias before relying on AI output. Several instruments specify that users must consult authoritative or original sources and cannot verify one model by asking the same or another AI system. The rationale rests on plausible but fabricated authorities, outdated information, factual mistakes and automation bias. Court cases involving nonexistent citations demonstrate concrete litigation consequences, but the materials generally do not measure model error rates. One qualification is that the Canadian guidance questions whether human verification will remain feasible for every evolving system, which strengthens the case for limiting use where meaningful verification cannot occur.

qs.q: VERIFICATION REQUIREMENT  7.1 Content produced using AI must be verified with meaningful human control.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: While some tools perform better than others, human verification of all AI and GenAI outputs remains essential for all judicial use cases.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Task-specific boundaries are replacing blanket bans, especially around evidence and consequential decisions.
kps.d: Courts generally distinguish lower-risk assistance from uses that threaten evidential authenticity or procedural fairness. Permitted or proposed uses include chronologies, indexes, summaries, preliminary drafts, proofreading, scheduling, translation and case-management analytics. Stricter rules apply to witness evidence, expert reports, detention, sentencing and other consequential decisions. New South Wales prohibits generating or rephrasing witness evidence while allowing merely preparatory work; Singapore permits a compliant first draft but prohibits fabrication or tampering; Victoria requires final evidence to remain in the witness's own knowledge and words. These differences show that the precise boundary between assistance and prohibited intervention remains jurisdiction-specific.

qs.q: Gen AI must not be used in generating the content of affidavits, witness       statements, character references or other material that is intended to reflect the       deponent or witness’ evidence and/or opinion, or other material tendered in       evidence or used in cross examination.
qs.a: Supreme Court of NSW Practice Note SC Gen 23 — Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (issued 28 January 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Asking a Generative AI tool to generate a first-cut draft                 of an affidavit/statement can be done (provided that this Guide is complied                 with), but it is not acceptable to ask a Generative AI to fabricate or tamper with                 evidence.
qs.a: Guide on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools by Court Users (Singapore Courts, Registrar's Circular No. 1 of 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Confidentiality and security controls turn on tool architecture, data handling and institutional control.
kps.d: The policies repeatedly distinguish public or externally controlled systems from private, closed or court-managed tools. Common controls prohibit entering confidential, privileged, personally identifiable, health, sealed or otherwise non-public information into public models; require review of contractual terms, privacy settings and retention practices for closed tools; and favour approved tools, secure work devices and institutional systems. Some regimes impose broader restrictions, such as New York's ban on uploading any filed court document to a non-private model even if the document is public. Practical implementation therefore requires procurement review, data classification, access controls, breach reporting and scrutiny of whether providers retain inputs or use them for training.

qs.q: No user may input into any generative AI program that does not operate on a private model —      by writing a prompt, uploading a document or file, or otherwise — any information that is      confidential, private, or privileged, or includes personally identifiable information or      protected health information, or is otherwise inappropriate for public release.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: 6.9 For closed AI tools:  (a) If Court users input private, confidential or sensitive information into closed AI tools they need to exercise caution and satisfy themselves by reviewing the contractual terms or privacy and confidentiality settings that the information they input will be kept within a secure environment.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Jurisdictions disagree most visibly over approval and disclosure, not over human responsibility.
kps.d: Internal court governance ranges from prior approval of particular tools or uses to general guidelines that allow use without case-by-case permission. Disclosure rules vary more sharply: Canada requires a declaration for AI-generated filing content; some US judges require disclosure, traceability or certification; New South Wales requires statements of non-use in specified witness documents; Victoria can demand identification and an account of verification; Singapore and Illinois reject routine advance disclosure in defined contexts. Contextual approaches ask whether disclosure affects provenance, evidential weight, client expectations or local ethical duties. Critics warn that fragmented standing orders can be vague, difficult to comply with and potentially deterrent, although the materials do not show that deterrence has occurred.

qs.q: Under this approach, court personnel do not need to obtain court approval for each type of AI usage, but if they choose to use AI, they must adhere to a set of guidelines and constraints.
qs.a: AI Readiness for the State Courts: A Guide for Courts · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: UCS users may use only those generative AI products that have been approved by the UCS      Division of Technology and Court Research (DoTCR), which are identified in the attached      Appendix.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Institutional governance must extend beyond individual verification to lifecycle oversight and contestability.
kps.d: Broader frameworks call for clear definitions, covered roles, permitted and prohibited uses, training, bias assessment, auditability, security, procurement controls, stakeholder participation and periodic revision. They also require courts to explain deployments, monitor outcomes and provide mechanisms for affected parties to challenge influential outputs. Human-centred design should respond to the needs and expertise of court staff and users rather than simply automate selected tasks and leave residual work to people. Approval alone does not establish safety; policies contemplate pilots, sandboxes and continuing impact assessments before and after deployment.

qs.q: As described above, the court should choose language that: 1) puts guardrails in place to mitigate risks in the short term and 2) clarifies for personnel which uses of AI are allowed or prohibited.
qs.a: AI Readiness for the State Courts: A Guide for Courts · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Accountability and contestability: Ensure accountability by informing and explaining               how and why certain AI tools were adopted by the judiciary and the results achieved (or               not) with their deployment.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Efficiency and access-to-justice benefits remain plausible but mostly unproven and may create new inequalities.
kps.d: Sources anticipate faster administration, reduced backlogs, clearer public communication, translation, support for self-represented litigants and more accessible online dispute resolution. Interviewed judges report or contemplate practical assistance with outlines, oral-argument preparation, plain-language summaries and forms, but the interview evidence is small and does not establish measured gains. Guidance also warns that self-represented litigants may lack the skills to detect errors and that AI-mediated services may exclude people without money, digital access or literacy. Autonomous adjudication remains speculative: some foresee consensual AI arbitration or small-claims applications, while others stress public resistance and the judiciary's constitutional and law-development roles.

qs.q: 1.3 AI can enhance access to justice and Court users' participation in Court processes.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: They discussed projects their court systems are considering, like user-friendly interfaces powered by GenAI that allow potential litigants, especially self-represented litigants, to receive guidance on topics (such as forms they may need to file).
qs.a: Judicial Use of Generative AI: Lessons Learned · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: The evidence base supports urgent governance more strongly than claims of operational effectiveness.
kps.d: Most materials are policies, practice notes, ethical guidance or forecasts rather than evaluations of deployed systems. They document concrete hallucination cases, reported judicial practices, comparative deployments and strong demand for guidance, but rarely quantify performance, workload effects, bias reduction or access outcomes. One global survey reports limited organisational guidance and strong support for mandatory regulation and training; a later judicial interview study provides qualitative experience from a small sample. Practical adoption should therefore pair experimentation with empirical validation, documented success measures and regularly revised rules rather than treat policy proliferation or reported use as proof of effectiveness.

qs.q: **Absence of Guidance and Training on AI**  There is a significant lack of guidance and training on AI usage is evident, with just 9% of judicial operators reporting that their organizations have issued guidelines or provided AI-related training.
qs.a: Global Judges' Initiative: Survey on the Use of AI Systems by Judicial Operators · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Background In October and November of 2025, 13 interviews of approximately 60 minutes in duration were conducted with state and federal judges serving in 10 different states.
qs.a: Judicial Use of Generative AI: Lessons Learned · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: The curated sources from regulators, courts and professional bodies accept the proposition’s core: AI may assist legal and judicial work, but adjudicative authority, professional duties and responsibility for outputs remain human. They commonly justify this position through the risks of fabricated or outdated material, bias, compromised evidential authenticity, confidentiality breaches and automation bias, making independent verification, secure tools and task-specific limits central safeguards. Collectively, the voice builds materially on the proposition by translating individual accountability into institutional governance across procurement, training, participatory design, auditability, contestability, pilots, impact assessment and periodic policy revision. Material variation concerns implementation rather than the core principle: some jurisdictions require prior tool approval while others rely on use guidelines; disclosure ranges from mandatory declarations or certifications to contextual disclosure or no routine advance disclosure; and evidentiary boundaries differ, particularly over AI-assisted witness drafting. A narrower practitioner primer does not clearly address court governance, and Canadian guidance qualifies the verification consensus by warning that meaningful human verification may become infeasible for some systems. Efficiency and access-to-justice benefits are generally treated as plausible but not yet well demonstrated. Because these are selected sources, this synthesis indicates the relationship within the supplied corpus and not the prevalence of these views among all institutions in this professional group.

qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Additionally, introduce mechanisms that allow affected parties               to contest and cross-examine any output produced by an AI system that may influence the               outcome of the case at hand, as well as challenge the decisions and hold judicial operators               accountable for their errors.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: Across this curated set, the academia and research sources support the proposition that court use of generative AI should remain assistive, task-bounded and subject to human accountability. Their common reasons are the need for professional oversight, independent verification, ethical compliance, transparency and tighter controls for evidentiary or otherwise consequential uses. They also broadly support the synthesis’s caution that published guidance is more developed than evidence of effective implementation or measurable benefits. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis: one source descriptively catalogues restrictions without establishing authorial endorsement; the ODR source cautiously anticipates access-to-justice benefits from early-stage informational assistance; the eDiscovery study makes acceptance conditional on empirical validation and risk-focused standards; the verification critique stresses lawyers’ personal and institutional consequences for unchecked output; and the Brazilian case study foregrounds uncertain training, implementation and protection of citizens’ rights. These are complementary qualifications rather than substantive opposition, and the sources do not collectively establish operational effectiveness or uniform rules across jurisdictions.

The supplied press source supports the proposition’s core assistive, human-accountable model. Reporting Conrad’s description of federal judiciary guidance, it presents AI as potentially useful but subject to firm limits: core judicial decision-making and adjudication should not be delegated, novel legal questions require particular caution, outputs should be independently verified, and users remain accountable for AI-assisted work. It also supports the synthesis’s account of jurisdictional variation by describing disclosure as discretionary and allowing individual courts to define permissible tasks for locally approved tools. Materially, however, this is second-hand reporting rather than an independent evaluation or direct analysis of the guidance: FedScoop did not obtain the underlying document, and the source offers no measured evidence of effectiveness. Because the curated evidence contains only this source in this professional-voice category, its position should not be generalized to market analysts, consultancies or the press as a whole.

qs.q: Some of the recommendations leave room for discretion, such as a recommendation to consider whether AI use should be disclosed.
qs.a: Interim AI guidance for US courts aims for experimentation with guardrails · Market & press · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core assistive, human-accountable model and materially develop it into a practical governance framework. Across court policies, judicial guidance and professional opinions, AI is permitted for support functions, but judges retain adjudicative authority and lawyers, litigants and court personnel remain responsible for work produced in their names. The common reasons are the risk of fabricated authorities and facts, confident but misplaced reliance, bias, confidentiality and security exposure, and the continuing force of existing legal and ethical duties. Verification is consequently treated as the principal operational safeguard, while evidence preparation and consequential decisions attract stricter task boundaries. Several sources go beyond individual checking by specifying procurement controls, approved tools, secure devices, training, explainability, pilots, impact assessment, monitoring and policy revision. Material internal variation concerns implementation rather than the accountability principle: Canada requires disclosure of AI-generated filing content, some US judges require disclosure, traceability or certification, and Victoria generally favours contextual disclosure, whereas Singapore and Illinois reject routine advance disclosure in defined contexts. Approval models likewise range from institutionally approved tools to generally authorized use subject to safeguards. The Canadian Judicial Council also qualifies the verification consensus by warning that verification may become infeasible for some evolving systems, supporting tighter limits where meaningful human checking cannot be performed. Claims of efficiency and access-to-justice benefits remain mostly prospective; most sources provide normative guidance, reported incidents or forecasts rather than measured operational outcomes. These relationships describe this curated set and should not be read as evidence of how prevalent each position is among courts or legal institutions generally.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core assistive, human-accountable model and materially develop it for institutional adoption at scale. Their common reasoning is that AI can support research, drafting, summarisation, document review and administration, but adjudicative authority, professional responsibility and direct engagement with evidence remain human. They operationalise that position through independent verification, approved-tool regimes, training, data-classification and security controls, defined permitted and prohibited tasks, and continuing legal and ethical duties. Several sources extend individual checking into lifecycle governance through participatory design, bias assessment, audit trails, institutional transparency and mechanisms for affected parties to contest influential AI outputs. Material variation concerns implementation rather than human responsibility: some jurisdictions require prior tool approval while others rely on general constraints; disclosure ranges from non-use statements for specified evidence to contextual or discretionary disclosure; and evidentiary boundaries differ in detail. The Law Society primer does not clearly address court governance, and the Brazilian case study stresses uncertainty about implementation and training. More broadly, these materials are predominantly policies, guidance and proposals—not evaluations—so they strengthen the case for scalable governance more than they establish productivity, access-to-justice or other operational gains. Duplicate or closely related records from the UK, New South Wales and the US federal judiciary should not be treated as separate evidence of prevalence.

qs.q: Additionally, introduce mechanisms that allow affected parties               to contest and cross-examine any output produced by an AI system that may influence the               outcome of the case at hand, as well as challenge the decisions and hold judicial operators               accountable for their errors.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources consistently support the proposition that legal and court AI should remain assistive, with lawyers, judges and court users retaining responsibility for decisions and work products. Common reasons are the risks of fabricated or inaccurate content, bias, confidentiality breaches and compromised evidential authenticity. Accordingly, the sources emphasise meaningful human verification against authoritative or original sources, careful limits around witness and expert evidence, restrictions on sensitive data in public tools, and continued application of existing professional and judicial duties. The principal internal variation concerns implementation rather than human accountability: some regimes require approved tools and prior training, while others provide non-binding or generally applicable guidance; disclosure ranges from certification or explanation requirements to contextual disclosure without a blanket advance declaration. The eDiscovery source is narrower and predictive, arguing that acceptance will depend on empirical validation and standards, while the judicial-interview evidence reports exploratory uses and anticipated access-to-justice or efficiency benefits without measuring those outcomes. Thus, the period strengthens the governance proposition but continues to support caution about claims of operational effectiveness.
